newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices climb as US farmers keep hold of crops.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices climb as US farmers keep hold of crops.

text.p: Wheat prices jumped Wednesday, boosted by tight stockpiles and farmers' reluctance to sell their crops following a prolonged slide in prices.
"The domestic wheat supplies are pretty tight. Throughout the fall farmer movement has been light," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for Chicago-based trade house FIMAT Futures.
Stronger wheat prices contributed to a rise of 0.68 points to 246.19 points in the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures contracts.
Natural gas was also among the day's strong gainers, settling at an all-time high, continuing its scorching rally on forecasts for cold weather.
Some traders saw a Moroccan purchase of Argentine wheat as a contributing factor in Wednesday's wheat rally because the sale was done at stronger prices than were seen recently.
A member of the Casablanca-based cereal importers committee said Wednesday Morocco bought 40,000 metric tons of Argentine soft wheat at $155 and $158 a ton for December delivery.
"I think it had something to do with the Moroccan sale (which was) up $5 per ton from where we heard world wheat values were," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.

December wheat jumped 15-1/2 cents to $4.13-1/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade, where prices for nearby months had dropped from a record high of $7.50 a bushel in late March to $3.68 earlier this month.
Natural gas prices continued to derive support from revised weather forecasts this week calling for mostly below-normal U.S. temperatures through the month which caught many by surprise.
Traders who took positions betting prices would fall have been trying to take cover and prices have surged 37 percent in the last five sessions.
"There's a short squeeze going on. Some people must have been caught big time and there's a lot of panic," said one Texas-based trader.
The December natural gas contract, which expires on Thursday, rose 32.1 cents to $3.627 for 1,000 cubic feet at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Oil prices seesawed in New York with gasoline leading the fall after an early advance.

Crude prices surged early in the session after the The American Petroleum Institute (API) said on Tuesday that crude stocks dropped 3.5 million barrels for the week ended November 15, putting stocks at a lean 9.9 million barrels below a year ago.
"The support from the APIs ran out of steam. Gasoline was the first to go, which led everything lower," said ING Derivatives analyst Tom Bentz.
Though the API reported a drop in gasoline stocks as well, traders noted the high output rate for gasoline undermined its price since it signalled stock builds in the future.
Gasoline output grew to 7.78 million barrels a day last week from 7.43 million barrels a day for the week ended November 8.
Traders said the decline accelerated as the breach of key technical price levels triggered chart-based selling.
December crude oil fell 73 cents to $23.76 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange after rising as high as $24.95.
Refined products were also hit hard with December gasoline losing two cents to 65.39 cents a gallon and December heating oil off 1.59 cents at 72.09 cents a gallon.
